turns.text: Earth Report, number one. To Command. Date, local reckoning: November eleventh, twenty twenty-six. I have arrived, sir. The planet is still running. <short pause> I cannot tell you how. The mission stands. Observe. Report. Do not get attached. Fourteen files from the last two days. Let's begin.

turns.text: File one: the war. Russia and Ukraine have been fighting for four and a half years. Yesterday they sat down in Abu Dhabi, with the Americans mediating, for the first time in nine months. Before the session, the Ukrainians and the Americans met the Europeans and NATO. The Kremlin had objected to that. So, a meeting before the meeting. To agree on what to say in the meeting. The session ran four hours. That is less than one hour per year of war. The Americans called it very productive. The Ukrainians called it constructive. Neither the American secretary of state nor the Ukrainian president was actually in the room. And there is no agreement. <short pause> On this planet, sir, a successful meeting is one that ends by scheduling another meeting. And yes. There is another one today. Meanwhile, Russia is hitting Ukraine's power grid as winter sets in. And this, sir, is not a joke. Cutting heat and light to civilians in the middle of winter is not a war plan. <short pause> It is a crime. They negotiate peace by day. And people sleep in the dark and the cold by night.

turns.text: File two: the United States. Their most powerful country. The House voted on a motion to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over the war with Iran. The count: 211 to 204. The motion was sent to a committee. A committee, sir, is where humans send things to die quietly. The motion came from a member of the president's own party. And more than a dozen members did not show up to vote. The secretary called it a farce, and sabotage. It was his first press briefing in six months. Six months of silence. First word back: farce. The president posted that the effort had miserably failed, and that the secretary was exonerated. Exonerated, with no trial. <short pause> Efficient. I took notes. The Pentagon called the result a total victory. A total victory. In a vote. <short pause> Apparently those are the wars they can still win. The opposition takes over the House in January. So this file will be back on my desk. Also: the United States skipped its human rights review at the United Nations. For the second year running. Not showing up is a policy here, sir. <short pause> For votes, and for reviews.

turns.text: File three. My personal favorite. France is accusing Iran of a cyberattack. On supermarket fridges. Hundreds of stores. The fridges heated themselves up overnight. The food spoiled, and in a few places there were fires. That was in October. Since then, similar incidents have turned up across Europe and beyond. France summoned the ambassador and says it rules nothing out. Iran says: not us. So, sir. Their weapons now target cheese. It stopped being funny this month: there was a failed attempt on the cooling units at French blood banks. Urgent recommendation: change the password on the ship's fridge.

On Sunday, three children and a woman died when a sand embankment collapsed onto their tents. People there say the rain comes at them from one side, and the sewage overflows from the other. A body called the Board of Peace says the aid Israel has let in is insufficient. Israel says it has let in tens of thousands of tents. I have no stake in their arguments, sir. Not their politics. Not their religions. <short pause> But children dying in flooded tents is not politics. It is a crime. These creatures are extremely good at writing statements. <short pause> A statement does not keep anyone warm. And for the record: what is being done to these civilians is wrong. <short pause> Whoever is doing it. Whatever reason they give.

And he is from this planet! <short pause> I am from another galaxy, and the only question anyone has asked me is where I got the hat. This planet is crawling with spies, sir. <short pause> We are going to need a bigger budget.

Five percent, one time only, on anyone worth more than a billion dollars. That is about two hundred people. It would have raised around a hundred billion dollars for healthcare. And the voters said: no. Even the governor opposed it. He was afraid the rich would leave. Experts say it would have been the first wealth tax on billionaires anywhere in the world. Some billionaires spent millions to kill the tax. A few left the state altogether. Millions of humans voted so that two hundred of them would not have to pay. <short pause> They call it trickle-down, sir. I have checked. Nothing is trickling.

And the first to pay, sir, are the poorest people on the planet. <short pause> The ones whose houses will not hold.
